mcqs.question: What is the correct order for diagnosing a SOLID violation live in an interview?
options: Name the letter first, then find lines in the code that match it
Name the smell in plain English first, then map it to a letter, then propose the fix
Propose a fix first, then justify it by naming a letter afterward
Ask the interviewer which letter they're testing for, then confirm it in the code
mcqs.explanation: Naming the letter before the smell is exactly how candidates confidently misdiagnose code — they pattern-match to the question's framing instead of what's actually there. Starting from the plain-English smell keeps the diagnosis grounded in the actual code, with the letter and fix following from it.

mcqs.question: A `Penguin(Bird)` subclass overrides `fly()` to raise `NotImplementedError`. What's the correct diagnosis and fix?
options: This is an SRP violation; fix it by splitting `Bird` into smaller classes
This is not a violation, since exceptions are a normal way to signal unsupported behavior
This is an LSP violation; fix it by removing `fly()` from `Bird` and introducing a `FlyingBird` subtype only flying birds implement
This is an OCP violation; fix it by adding a new `elif` branch for penguins wherever `fly()` is called
mcqs.explanation: Any code calling `bird.fly()` polymorphically breaks the moment it receives a `Penguin` — the subclass can't honor the contract the base class promises, which is exactly what LSP names. Splitting responsibilities (SRP) or branching by type (OCP-style) don't address the substitutability problem, and raising on an unsupported method is the violation, not an acceptable pattern.

mcqs.question: When asked to refactor a violation live in a two-minute window, what should you actually produce?
options: A narrated plan for the shape of the fix, with just the key interface and one implementation sketched, not full working code
Complete, fully working code for every class in the fix, skipping the narration to save time
Only a verbal description with no code sketched at all, since two minutes is too short to write anything
A request to skip the refactor and move to the next question, since two minutes isn't realistic
mcqs.explanation: Interviewers are scoring whether your plan's shape is sound, not whether you can produce working code in two minutes — sketching the key interface and one implementation while narrating the rest demonstrates the plan without wasting the clock on ceremony. Full code is unrealistic in the window, and giving nothing (verbal-only or declining) wastes a chance to show the design.

mcqs.question: A candidate calls a clean, single-purpose `Order` class an SRP violation, reasoning "it has four methods, so that's too many." What's wrong with this diagnosis?
options: Nothing — four methods is a well-known threshold past which SRP is always violated
SRP only applies to classes with fewer than four methods, so the diagnosis doesn't apply here
The diagnosis is right, but the fix proposed afterward would be wrong
Method count isn't a responsibility signal; naming a violation that isn't there is worse than saying the code looks clean
mcqs.explanation: Method count alone says nothing about whether those methods represent separate reasons to change — a class can have many cohesive methods serving one responsibility. Confidently naming a false violation to sound sharp reads worse in an interview than correctly saying the code looks clean; there's no four-method threshold or class-size cutoff for SRP.
